title: What happened at the close
text: Today the S&P 500 fund SPY ended at $769.49, down 0.37%. The Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ fell 1.41% to $715.41. The big story was Alphabet, which dropped 12.6% to $283.82 after its report. Amazon fell 4.2% before its own report came out after the close, and Eli Lilly jumped 6.6%. Tomorrow, watch how Amazon trades after its results and whether the AI group steadies. This is for learning, not advice.

title: Alphabet's big one day drop
text: Alphabet fell 12.6% to $283.82 after its third quarter report. Reports say profit per share was $2.12, well below the $3.02 analysts expected. Its spending on AI equipment was bigger than the cash its business brought in. Its cloud business grew very fast, but search growth was slower than hoped. The stock is now 31% below its 52 week high of $408.61.

title: Amazon: faster cloud, nervous investors
text: Amazon closed at $243.79, down 4.2%, as worries about AI spending grew. After the close, Amazon reported that its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, its fastest pace in nearly five years. Profit per share of $1.89 came in a bit under what analysts expected. Reports disagree on how far the stock moved after hours, so check the open before drawing conclusions.

title: Eli Lilly rises on a raised forecast
text: Eli Lilly gained 6.6% to $1,373 after it beat expectations and raised its sales forecast for the year. Sales rose 39% to $24.4 billion, led by its diabetes and weight loss medicines. Lilly's beta is 0.45, so it usually moves less than the market, which makes a 6.6% jump unusual.

title: Lesson 29: What is capex?
text: Capex is short for capital expenditure. It is the money a company spends on big things it will use for years, like buildings, machines and computer chips. Think of a pizza shop that buys a new oven. The oven costs a lot today, but it can make pizzas for years. Right now, giant tech companies are spending tens of billions of dollars on data centers for AI. That can help them grow later, but it also leaves less cash in the bank today. This week, Alphabet's capex was bigger than the cash its business brought in, and investors did not like that. When you read about a company, check both how much it spends and what it earns from that spending.
